source.title: Scaling Sentence Embeddings with Large Language Models
source.authors: Ting Jiang; Shao-Han Huang; Zhong-Zhi Luan; De-Qing Wang; Fu-Zhen Zhuang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports how downstream sentence-embedding task scores vary with model size, extending scaling analysis to this task setting. It does not test held-out pretraining cross-entropy or compute-optimal training allocations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports downstream STS and transfer-task scores across model sizes and representation/training settings. These bear on V6. Its results are not measurements of held-out pretraining loss, power-law fits, small-run extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocations. The reported averages are retained as aggregates; the per-dataset scores are not expanded into separate rows.
record.test_reason: Research question 3 asks whether scaling still helps beyond billions of parameters. The study evaluates pretrained OPT (125M–66B) and LLaMA (7B–65B) on downstream sentence-embedding tasks (STS, transfer) with a fixed representation method across sizes. That bears on V6 in a new task setting. It fits no scaling curve and reports no pretraining loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find that going from millions to billions of parameters improves STS, but further scaling does not help and may harm it: 66B OPT underperforms 6.7B OPT even with ICL. Transfer tasks improve with size, and 66B OPT / 65B LLaMA are best. ICL gains grow with size. After contrastive fine-tuning, 2.7B OPT beats 4.8B ST5, and gains from 2.7B to 13B are not significant.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates sentence-embedding STS and transfer scores across model sizes and representation/training settings; it does not measure held-out pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with task (STS versus transfer), model size, representation method, in-context demonstrations, and fine-tuning. The paper reports that in-context learning substantially improves STS scores but task-irrelevant examples do not improve transfer results.

fits_no_version.finding: The share of in-context demonstrations that improve STS-B dev performance rises sharply with size: one demonstration helps 125M OPT, about 98% help 2.7B. ICL gains also grow with size (e.g. +9.35 at 66B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of in-context demonstrations for sentence embeddings grows with model size (scale-dependent ICL ability).

fits_no_version.finding: Adding ICL or contrastive NLI fine-tuning lowers transfer-task averages relative to plain PromptEOL at most sizes (Table 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-mismatched adaptation can offset scale gains on downstream probes.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), 2023
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the tabulated scores. The tested outcomes are downstream sentence-embedding metrics, not pretraining loss; the study does not fit or validate predictive scaling curves.
record.rows_left_out: Per-dataset scores and additional representation-method comparisons were not entered separately; the table-level aggregate averages are recorded instead. Quantization comparisons and transfer-task results for ICL/CSE settings are omitted because the selected rows already capture the principal model-size trends and condition-dependent STS versus transfer pattern.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss measured or fitted.
No fits on small runs and no extrapolation.
No architecture-shape variation at fixed size.
No loss power laws in other modalities or regimes; fine-tuning here is reported only as downstream scores.
No fitted predictive relation (e.g. power law in size) and no relation to pretraining loss; only raw scores by size.

missing.what: PromptEOL transfer averages for OPT 125M (86.23) and 350M (86.78); these extend the transfer scaling series downward.
PromptEOL+CSE STS averages for OPT 125M (81.69) and 350M (82.33); these extend the fine-tuned series.
STS-B dev Spearman across OPT 125M–66B for three representation methods; shows size dependence varies with the representation method.

record.verdict_notes: Every row was marked 'partial' regardless of trend; states are reassigned per position in each size series. Scores come from the authors' own PromptEOL method, and ICL demonstrations are tuned per model on the STS-B dev set, which confounds size comparisons and overlaps with the STS-B test task. No uncertainty is reported, so small differences (<1 point) may be noise. Table 8's 'unsupervised' heading appears to label the supervised CSE results. The study cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. but is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute, and power-law behavior over several orders of magnitude.
Whether power laws fit on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study measures downstream sentence-embedding scores across model sizes, but does not fit a predictive scaling relationship or relate these scores to pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices, setup, or parameter-counting; no loss curves or exponents are fitted.

relationships.condition: Transfer tasks (logistic-regression probes) with PromptEOL, OPT 1.3B–66B and LLaMA 7B–65B
relationships.reason: Average accuracy rises with size and the largest models are best (OPT 89.87→91.45, LLaMA 91.06→92.09); the authors say transfer improves with size. Rows r23–r32.
relationships.display_finding: Average transfer accuracy increased from 89.87 to 91.45 for OPT and 91.06 to 92.09 for LLaMA, with the largest models performing best.

relationships.condition: STS without fine-tuning (PromptEOL and PromptEOL+ICL), OPT 125M–66B
relationships.reason: Gains appear only from millions to about 1–7B params, non-monotonically (350M and 2.7B dips without ICL), then stop. Rows r1–r16.
relationships.display_finding: Gains stopped around 1–7B parameters, with intermediate declines at 350M and 2.7B without in-context learning.

relationships.condition: STS without fine-tuning, OPT above ~1.3B (no ICL) or ~6.7B (ICL)
relationships.reason: The largest model scores lower: 66B 68.84 vs 1.3B 73.18 without ICL; 66B 78.19 vs 6.7B 79.08 with ICL. The authors say scaling past tens of billions harms STS. Rows r4–r8, r14–r16.
relationships.display_finding: Without in-context learning, 66B scored 68.84 versus 73.18 at 1.3B; with in-context learning, 66B scored 78.19 versus 79.08 at 6.7B.

relationships.condition: STS after supervised contrastive QLoRA fine-tuning, OPT 1.3B–13B and LLaMA 7B–13B
relationships.reason: Scores rise monotonically but saturate (OPT 85.62→85.97 from 2.7B to 13B; LLaMA 85.70→85.85); the authors call the gain not significant. Rows r17–r22.
relationships.display_finding: Fine-tuned scores rose only from 85.62 to 85.97 for OPT 2.7B–13B and from 85.70 to 85.85 for LLaMA 7B–13B, gains the authors considered insignificant.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Transfer-task averages for OPT and LLaMA using PromptEOL
reader_labels.reason: Average transfer performance is generally higher for larger models, and the authors state that scaling improves transfer-task performance; see r23–r32.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: STS averages across OPT sizes, including in-context learning and supervised contrastive fine-tuning
reader_labels.reason: STS scores are not consistently monotonic with size: the no-demonstration 66B OPT score is below several smaller models, and the ICL series peaks at 6.7B before declining; the authors also describe scaling beyond tens of billions as potentially harmful on STS. Fine-tuned gains are small at larger sizes.
